extracted.intended_audience: researchers, funders, publishers and others interested in open peer review and open research publishing (including Wellcome grantholders)
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of the post-publication, invited peer review model used at Wellcome Open Research (WOR), including process rules, quality checks, reviewer selection/conflict management, outcome categories, metrics on reviewer behaviour, and timeliness. Useful for people evaluating or implementing open, transparent peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate publication after editorial checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions are subjected to a range of editorial checks (e.g., plagiarism detection, checking the data availability statement, and ensuring that the appropriate ethical standards have been adhered to). Once these checks have been completed – and any issues addressed – the article is published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial checks are performed before publication rather than as part of reviewer gatekeeping; publication occurs once these checks and any fixes are done.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-publication invited peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: On publication, the reviewers – as suggested by the corresponding author – are formally invited to review the article. Reviews are conducted after the article is publicly available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the research is already published, reviewers can focus on providing help and advice on improving the article and on highlighting errors or omissions rather than acting as a pre-publication gatekeeper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer identity and review transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: All reviews are citable and posted to the platform along with the identities of the reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full disclosure of reviewer identity and their review text is intended to increase transparency and accountability (‘sunshine is the best disinfectant’). This visibility is expected to minimise potential misuse of author-suggested reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer recommendation categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers indicate whether the work as presented should be “approved,” “approved with reservations” or “not approved.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each review includes a narrative plus one of the three status labels. These labels are used as explicit evaluative signals about the article's acceptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for indexing in PubMed and bibliographic databases
rubrics_metrics.description: Only submissions that receive two “approved” statuses or one “approved” and two “approved with reservations” are indexed in PubMed and other bibliographic databases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indexing depends on the combination of published reviewer statuses rather than a single editor decision; authors may need to obtain multiple positive/qualified reviews to achieve indexing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author-suggested reviewers (author-initiated peer review)
rubrics_metrics.description: The platform allows the authors to suggest reviewers, on the logic that they are often best placed to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While author suggestion speeds identification of reviewers, it raises concerns about potential bias (authors suggesting friendly reviewers). The model relies on transparency and declaration of associations to minimise risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest declaration and screening
rubrics_metrics.description: All reviewers are required to declare any associations with the author(s). F1000 staff also seek to identify obvious conflicts, such as checking PubMed to determine if any authors have collaborated recently with the reviewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflict management combines self-declaration and editorial checks; the public disclosure of reviewer identity and their declared associations further mitigates concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeatable peer review for new versions
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors can submit a new version of the article – either to address comments from reviewers or to update the publication in light of any new findings – and the peer review process is repeated for each new version.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Versioning allows iterative improvement and re-evaluation; each version accumulates its own set of published reviews and status labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusive scope of publishable outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: WOR provides a platform for publishing any research finding that a Wellcome-funded researcher wishes to share. This includes traditional research articles, but also outputs such as data notes, protocols, method papers, software tools and null and negative results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The platform's acceptance policy emphasises a broad set of scholarly outputs beyond conventional articles, supporting reproducibility and sharing of diverse research products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer behaviour and willingness to criticise (observed statistics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical observation from Year 1: around 35% of Version 1 articles were “approved with reservations,” and 2% of reviewer reports applied the “not approved” status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These published proportions are used as evidence that author-suggested, named reviewers still provide substantive critique and will put their name to critical reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer recruitment effort metric
rubrics_metrics.description: To reach indexed status, on average 11 reviewers were approached. The median number of reviewers contacted to achieve indexed status is nine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The model may require approaching multiple potential reviewers; these numbers quantify the typical outreach burden to secure the necessary reviews for indexing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness metric (publication workflow duration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis conducted in November 2017 showed that on average articles completed the entire publication workflow in 72 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post-publication invited-review model plus the editorial checks did not substantially increase elapsed time to indexing in observed Year 1 data; 72 days is the measured average from submission through peer review/indexing milestones.
